assessment.nobel_worthiness: Topological insulators are a genuinely new state of matter: an insulating bulk with protected conducting boundary states. The theory (Kane-Mele Z2 invariant, Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal) and experiment (HgTe quantum wells, then Bi-Sb and Bi2Se3 surface states by ARPES) fit together, and first-principles band-structure calculations were central to identifying materials. This is the kind of quantum surprise in materials that I value.
assessment.attribution: Kane (with Mele) supplied the decisive theory of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group made the first experimental observation in HgTe; Hasan's ARPES work established the 3D case. Eugene Mele is a co-originator of the Kane-Mele work and cannot be included in a trio, and Bernevig, Zhang, Fu and Moore are not in the supplied credit, so allocation is contested.
assessment.maturity: More than fifteen years of independent confirmation across many materials, transport and spectroscopy, with a stable interpretation. Timing is ripe, and the 2016 prize on topological phase transitions does not cover this discovery.
uncertainties: Which three of Kane, Mele, Molenkamp and Hasan is fairest is unresolved.
Important theory contributors (Bernevig, Zhang, Fu, Moore) fall outside the supplied credited names.
Practical applications remain limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened moire flat-band physics: correlated insulators, superconductivity and later Chern and fractional states in a tunable platform. Theory predicted the flat bands at a magic angle and experiment found the correlated phases, a fine example of a surprise from graphene, which I know well from the 2010 prize.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands and the magic angle; Jarillo-Herrero's group reported the correlated insulator and superconductivity. Cao and others in the experimental team, and Santos, Lopes dos Santos and Peres in early theory, are outside the credit, so the trio is clean but not complete.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups, and the field has grown into a major area. The nature of the superconductivity and of the correlated states is still debated, so the interpretation is not fully settled; recognition would be timely but slightly early.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity and correlated states is still debated.
Sample-dependence and twist-angle disorder complicate reproducibility.
Early theory contributors and the leading student experimentalist are not in the credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magnetic skyrmions in chiral magnets are a topological magnetic texture with emergent electrodynamics, observed by neutron scattering and real-space imaging, and linked to the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction that I treat with first-principles and atomistic spin-dynamics methods. Clear physical discovery with a possible link to spintronics.
assessment.attribution: Pfleiderer's group found the skyrmion lattice in MnSi by neutron scattering, and Tokura's group imaged it in real space and explored the emergent electromagnetism. The theory pioneers (Bogdanov, Rossler, Bishop) and other experimentalists are missing from the credit, which makes the prize configuration difficult.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many techniques and materials over fifteen years. Room-temperature skyrmions exist, but technological use is still limited, so the practical case is not yet made.
uncertainties: Allocation to theory pioneers such as Bogdanov is unresolved.
Application impact is not yet demonstrated.
Tokura appears on other candidate entries, which may be a concern for overlap.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices gives controlled realisations of Hubbard-type models, such as the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and, later, single-site resolution. It provides clean tests of many-body theory I care about and ties to condensed-matter questions.
assessment.attribution: The Jaksch-Zoller proposal and the Greiner-Bloch Mott-insulator experiment are the decisive early contributions; Esslinger's Fermi-Hubbard work and Cirac's proposals also matter. Five names are credited, so a trio must omit significant contributors.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently confirmed by many labs, with a stable interpretation. The 2001 and 2012 prizes already covered related ground (condensates and single-quantum-system control), so novelty relative to them needs examination.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier cold-atom prizes.
Credit allocation among five contributors is difficult.
Simulation results for the hardest correlated regimes are still being validated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance, and later giant TMR in MgO junctions, underpins magnetic read heads and MRAM. It is a clear device-relevant discovery in magnetism, linked to spin-dependent tunnelling and band-structure symmetry filtering, which first-principles theory predicted.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin and Yuasa/Djayaprawira reported giant MgO TMR in 2004. The theory of coherent tunnelling (Butler, Mathon, Umerski) is not among the supplied names, and Yuasa and Djayaprawira are also missing.
assessment.maturity: Widely replicated and commercial for years. Timing is mature, though the 2007 GMR prize covers closely related spintronics territory.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2007 GMR prize.
Key theory and MgO experiment credits are missing from the list.
Impact is mostly technological, not a new physical state.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory is the standard framework for strongly correlated electrons, and with DFT (DFT+DMFT) it gives quantitative spectra and phase diagrams of real materials. It is a methodological advance of lasting importance that I know well from the electronic-structure side.
assessment.attribution: Metzner and Vollhardt introduced the infinite-dimension limit; Georges and Kotliar built the DMFT mapping to the impurity problem, and Kotliar developed DFT+DMFT. Metzner and Rozenberg, Krauth and others are outside the credit; Georges, Kotliar and Vollhardt are plausible but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Widely used and benchmarked against experiment for three decades. Its interpretation is stable, though it is an approximation controlled mainly in infinite dimensions, and the Nobel tradition favours discoveries over computational methods.
uncertainties: Whether a theory method fits the prize criteria better than a discovery.
Metzner's contribution is not in the credited names.
Accuracy limits for low-dimensional systems.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reach 10^-18 fractional uncertainty, using the magic-wavelength idea and Sr or Yb atoms, and enable tests of fundamental physics and relativistic geodesy. A clear, quantitative, reproducible achievement in precision measurement.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice clock and realised it; Ye's group pushed it to the 10^-18 level. The credit is a clean pair, though others at NIST, JILA and PTB also contributed.
assessment.maturity: Independently confirmed by several laboratories with direct comparisons. The Hall and Haensch 2005 prize and the Wineland 2012 prize are adjacent, so the case rests on a new level of precision rather than a new principle.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with prior precision-spectroscopy prizes.
Redefinition of the second has not yet happened.
Other groups contributed to the clock results.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism is a proposed third class of collinear magnetic order with momentum-dependent spin splitting without net magnetization, and it sits in my own field of magnetism and first-principles theory. It is conceptually fresh, and DFT calculations were central to identifying candidate materials.
assessment.attribution: The Smejkal-Sinova-Jungwirth group formulated the symmetry classification and the name; earlier related work (e.g. Hayami, Yuan and others) is not among the credited names. The trio is plausible but priority questions exist.
assessment.maturity: Spectroscopic evidence (ARPES, XMCD) in MnTe and CrSb is recent and still accumulating; the field is only a few years old. Recognition now would be premature.
uncertainties: Premature, given the limited independent confirmation.
Priority relative to earlier symmetry-based predictions.
Technological relevance is not established.
